hints: Focus on the words deletion of one nucleotide from the middle, not a whole codon of three nucleotides.
Remember mRNA is read in groups of three bases called codons, so ask yourself what happens to every group after one base is missing.
walkthrough:
**Spot what kind of change this is**

Great start, let's read carefully. One single nucleotide is deleted from the middle of the transcript. This is not a swap, it is a loss of one base.

Since codons are read in threes, losing one base is very disruptive.

**Apply the frameshift idea**

Think of the mRNA as a sentence read in 3-letter words. If you delete one letter in the middle, every 3-letter word after that point is regrouped.

This is called a frameshift mutation. All the codons from the deletion onwards will be different, so many different amino acids will be coded.

**Link to the protein**

A different amino acid sequence means different R groups, different bonds, and a different shape and function. So the effect is much bigger than just one amino acid change.

options.A: Degeneracy can sometimes rescue a substitution, but a single-base deletion shifts the whole reading frame so the protein is very unlikely to stay unchanged.
options.B: This assumes only one amino acid changes, which is wrong for a deletion. Many amino acids change, so tertiary structure is very likely to be affected.
options.C: This also assumes only one amino acid changes. A single nucleotide deletion causes a frameshift, changing all amino acids downstream, not just one.
options.D: Correct and well done. Deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon from the deletion onwards is regrouped and codes for a different amino acid sequence.
